summary: The IPv6 addressing architecture includes a unicast interface identifier used in creating many IPv6 addresses, and these identifiers are formed by a variety of methods. This document clarifies that the bits in an interface identifier have no meaning and that the whole identifier should be treated as an opaque value.

eli5.summary: The second half of an IPv6 address is like a house name. This says do not try to read secrets into the letters; just treat it as a name.

questions: do ipv6 interface identifier bits have meaning
should i parse an ipv6 interface id
what are the u and g bits in an ipv6 iid
subtitle: The last 64 bits of an IPv6 address are just an opaque value: do not read meaning into them.

tldr.problem: IPv6 addresses end in an Interface Identifier (IID), and the "u" and "g" bits inside it came from MAC addresses. As more ways of forming IIDs appeared, it was unclear whether those bits meant anything.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC says the bits in an IID have no generic meaning, so third parties must treat the whole IID as an opaque bit string. The u and g bits matter only when an IID is derived from an IEEE address.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4291 is updated: Modified EUI-64 format is required only when the IID is derived from an IEEE MAC-layer address, and new IID formats are free to use all 64 bits as they like.

facts.label: u bit position
facts.value: Position 6 in the IID (70 in the address)

facts.label: g bit position
facts.value: Position 7 in the IID (71 in the address)

today: RFC 7136 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4291; the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It tells implementers to treat the IID as an opaque value.

sections.title: Interface Identifiers and the u and g Bits
sections.content:
An IPv6 unicast address is a prefix followed by an Interface Identifier (IID). The IID is supposed to be unique on the links reached by routing to that prefix. RFC 4291 required 64-bit IIDs to be built in Modified EUI-64 format, which normally means transforming an Ethernet-style MAC address.

That format keeps two bits from the MAC address. The u/l bit says whether the address has universal or local scope; in the IID it is called the u bit and its value is inverted (1 for universal, 0 for local). The i/g bit marks group addressing and is kept as the g bit. In the IID they sit at position 6 and 7, which are positions 70 and 71 of the whole address when counting from 0.
sections.eli5: Many IPv6 addresses end with a name made from a network card's serial number. Two tiny switches in that name came from the card, and people wondered if the switches mean something.

sections.title: Why the Bits Have No Reliable Meaning
sections.content:
Many ways of forming an IID now exist besides the MAC-based one: temporary addresses, Cryptographically Generated Addresses, Hash-Based Addresses and ISATAP addresses, among others. Each sets the u and g bits differently. For example, RFC 3972 sets both to zero in CGAs, while RFC 4941 requires u to be zero but leaves g variable. Manually assigned small numbers for well-known servers also give zeros. The /127 prefixes of RFC 6164 do not even have a 64-bit IID.

The original hope was that universally unique IIDs would be useful, for instance for multihoming. That has not happened. MAC addresses with universal scope are sometimes assigned to several interfaces, and virtual machine environments reuse virtual MAC addresses. An IID with u = 1 may therefore claim to be universally unique while being ambiguous. Even ILNP, which might have benefited, defines its own Node Identifier instead.

The conclusion is that the u bit is not a reliable sign of uniqueness, and the g bit has no particular meaning either. Using the bits when generating an IID from a MAC address is fine; the point is that after an IID exists, no reliable deductions can be drawn from them.
sections.eli5: People copied the switches in different ways, and some name tags were copied by mistake onto two cards. So the switches cannot tell you whether a name is truly one of a kind.

sections.title: What the Bits Are Still Good For
sections.content:
If an IID is known or guessed to have been made under RFC 4291, it can be turned back into a MAC address. That helps with fault diagnosis, so mapping the IEEE bits into the IID keeps operational value. But an IID with u = 1 and g = 0 might equally come from another method, and other methods have no reverse transformation.

Because the bits carry no meaning, new IID formation methods may use them freely, for example as extra pseudo-random bits that reduce the chance of duplicate IIDs.
sections.eli5: If you know a name was built from a card's serial number, you can work backwards to find the card. But you cannot assume every name was built that way.

sections.title: Duplicate Address Detection
sections.content:
Duplicate Address Detection (DAD, RFC 4862) catches any case where two IIDs collide on the same link and produce a duplicate address. DAD can be extended across several links by a DAD proxy (RFC 6957) or by Neighbor Discovery Optimization (RFC 6775). Since DAD is mandatory for all nodes, almost no IID collision goes unnoticed.

What to do after a DAD failure is mostly out of scope and left to the implementation. If a manually created or MAC-derived IID fails, human intervention will most likely be needed. If the IID was not based on a hardware address, operation may continue once a new IID is created, for example by repeating a pseudo-random process.
sections.eli5: When two houses on the same street get the same name, the neighbours notice right away. Then one of them has to pick a new name.

sections.title: The Clarifications to RFC 4291
sections.content:
The RFC makes these requirements:

  • The EUI-64 to IID transformation of RFC 4291 MUST be used whenever an IID is derived from an IEEE MAC or EUI-64 address. For other link-layer addresses an equivalent transformation SHOULD be used.
  • Specifications of other 64-bit IID forms MUST say how all 64 bits are set, but MUST NOT define a generic meaning for the u and g bits. A method for a specific link type MAY give some bits local significance.
  • The whole IID MUST be viewed as an opaque bit string by third parties, except possibly in the local context.

Two edits follow. The sentence in Section 2.5.1 requiring Modified EUI-64 format for all IIDs is replaced by one that requires it only if the IID is derived from an IEEE MAC-layer address. The sentence saying the universal/local bit allows future technology to use universal-scope identifiers is obsoleted. As far as is known, no existing implementation is affected.
sections.eli5: If your name comes from a card's serial number, build it the usual way. Otherwise make it however you like, and everyone else should treat it as a plain name.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The RFC raises no new security exposures. It notes that unpredictable IID values are sometimes wanted to enhance privacy and defeat scanning attacks, and that treating the IID as opaque fits methods that produce pseudo-random values.

IANA is asked to do nothing immediately. A note was added to the "Reserved IPv6 Interface Identifiers" registry: a new reserved IID value would require updating IID generation code in every deployed IPv6 stack, so the justification for the required Standards Action would need to be extremely strong.
sections.eli5: Hard-to-guess names are good for privacy, and treating names as plain names fits that. Adding special reserved names would be costly, so there needs to be a very good reason.

viz.caption: THE TWO BITS INSIDE THE INTERFACE IDENTIFIER

items.title: u bit
items.text: Position 6 of the IID (position 70 of the address). Inverted from the MAC u/l bit: 1 means universal, 0 means local.

items.title: g bit
items.text: Position 7 of the IID (position 71 of the address). Copied from the MAC i/g bit, which marks group addressing.
